title: Navagraha Stotram
author: Traditional
description: A nine-verse hymn honoring the nine grahas as sacred archetypal forces of rhythm, karma, and contemplative alignment.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
जपाकुसुमसङ्काशं काश्यपेयं महद्युतिम्।
तमोऽरिं सर्वपापघ्नं प्रणतोऽस्मि दिवाकरम्॥
verses.transliteration:
japākusuma saṅkāśaṁ kāśyapeyaṁ mahadyutim
tamo'riṁ sarvapāpaghnaṁ praṇato'smi divākaram
verses.wordMeanings: japākusuma—hibiscus flower; saṅkāśam—radiant like; kāśyapeyam—descended from Kashyapa; mahā-dyutim—great splendor; tamo-ariṁ—enemy of darkness; sarva-pāpa-ghnam—destroyer of accumulated impurity; praṇataḥ asmi—I bow; divākaram—to the maker of the day.
verses.translation: I bow to the day-maker Surya, radiant like the hibiscus flower, born of Kashyapa, of great brilliance, enemy of darkness, and remover of accumulated impurity.
verses.commentary: The Surya verse frames the sun as illumination, rhythm, and moral clarity. On Sadhaka this is read not as fatalistic remedy language, but as a contemplative reminder to align with light, steadiness, and truthful action.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
दधिशङ्खतुषाराभं क्षीरोदार्णवसम्भवम्।
नमामि शशिनं सोमं शम्भोर्मुकुटभूषणम्॥
verses.transliteration:
dadhiśaṅkha tuṣārābhaṁ kṣīrodārṇava sambhavam
namāmi śaśinaṁ somaṁ śambhor mukuṭa bhūṣaṇam
verses.wordMeanings: dadhi—curd; śaṅkha—conch; tuṣāra—snow; ābham—shining like; kṣīroda-arṇava—ocean of milk; sambhavam—arisen from; namāmi—I bow; śaśinam—to the moon-marked one; somam—to Soma; śambhoḥ—of Shiva; mukuṭa-bhūṣaṇam—the ornament of the crown.
verses.translation: I bow to Soma, shining like curd, conch, and snow, arisen from the ocean of milk, and adorning Shiva's crown as the moon.
verses.commentary: Chandra is associated here with cooling, nourishment, and reflective mind. The image of the moon on Shiva's crown suggests emotion held within awareness rather than emotion ruling awareness.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
धरनीगर्भसम्भूतं विद्युत्कान्तिसमप्रभम्।
कुमारं शक्तिहस्तं तं मङ्गलं प्रणमाम्यहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
dharanīgarbha sambhūtaṁ vidyutkānti samaprabham
kumāraṁ śaktihastaṁ taṁ maṅgalaṁ praṇamāmyaham
verses.wordMeanings: dharanī-garbha—from the womb of earth; sambhūtam—born; vidyut-kānti—lightning brilliance; sama-prabham—equally radiant; kumāram—youthful one; śakti-hastam—holding a spear; maṅgalam—to Mangala; praṇamāmi aham—I bow.
verses.translation: I bow to Mangala, born from the womb of earth, radiant like lightning, youthful, and holding the spear of directed force.
verses.commentary: Mangala is presented as disciplined force and active courage. Rather than treating Mars symbolism as a fate-marker, this verse can be used to cultivate steadier action, cleaner boundaries, and courageous service.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
प्रियङ्गुकलिकाश्यामं रूपेणाप्रतिमं बुधम्।
सौम्यं सौम्यगुणोपेतं तं बुधं प्रणमाम्यहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
priyaṅgu kalikā śyāmaṁ rūpeṇāpratimaṁ budham
saumyaṁ saumya guṇopetaṁ taṁ budhaṁ praṇamāmyaham
verses.wordMeanings: priyaṅgu-kalikā—like the bud of the priyaṅgu plant; śyāmam—dark-green hued; rūpeṇa—in form; apratimam—matchless; budham—to Budha; saumyam—gentle; guṇa-upetam—endowed with qualities; praṇamāmi aham—I bow.
verses.translation: I bow to Budha, dark-green like a fresh bud, incomparable in form, gentle, and endowed with refined qualities.
verses.commentary: Budha represents language, discernment, and adaptive intelligence. This verse can orient the mind toward careful speech, clear study, and ethical analysis instead of scattered mental speed.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
देवानां च ऋषीणां च गुरुं काञ्चनसन्निभम्।
बुद्धिभूतं त्रिलोकेशं तं नमामि बृहस्पतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
devānāṁ ca ṛṣīṇāṁ ca guruṁ kāñcana sannibham
buddhibhūtaṁ trilokeśaṁ taṁ namāmi bṛhaspatim
verses.wordMeanings: devānām—of the devas; ṛṣīṇām—of the sages; gurum—the teacher; kāñcana-sannibham—golden in appearance; buddhi-bhūtam—embodiment of wisdom; triloka-īśam—lordly in the three worlds; namāmi—I bow; bṛhaspatim—to Brihaspati.
verses.translation: I bow to Brihaspati, teacher of gods and sages, golden in radiance, embodiment of wisdom, and revered guide across the three worlds.
verses.commentary: Brihaspati is the guru principle—guidance, ethics, blessings, and interpretive clarity. In practice this can mean honoring teachers, studying seriously, and choosing expansion through wisdom rather than appetite.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
हिमकुन्दमृणालाभं दैत्यानां परमं गुरुम्।
सर्वशास्त्रप्रवक्तारं भार्गवं प्रणमाम्यहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
himakunda mṛṇālābhaṁ daityānāṁ paramaṁ gurum
sarvaśāstra pravaktāraṁ bhārgavaṁ praṇamāmyaham
verses.wordMeanings: hima—snow; kunda—jasmine; mṛṇāla—lotus fiber; ābham—shining like; daityānām—of the asuras; paramam—supreme; gurum—teacher; sarva-śāstra-pravaktāram—speaker of all teachings; bhārgavam—to Shukra; praṇamāmi aham—I bow.
verses.translation: I bow to Shukra, radiant like snow, jasmine, and lotus fiber, supreme teacher of the asuras, and eloquent knower of all teachings.
verses.commentary: Shukra here is refinement, value, beauty, and relational intelligence. Spiritually, the verse reminds practitioners to refine desire into appreciation, gratitude, and ethical participation in the world.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
नीलाञ्जनसमाभासं रविपुत्रं यमाग्रजम्।
छायामार्तण्डसम्भूतं तं नमामि शनैश्चरम्॥
verses.transliteration:
nīlāñjana samābhāsaṁ raviputraṁ yamāgrajam
chāyāmārtaṇḍa sambhūtaṁ taṁ namāmi śanaiścaram
verses.wordMeanings: nīla-añjana—dark collyrium; sama-ābhāsam—shining like; ravi-putram—son of the sun; yama-agrajam—elder brother of Yama; chāyā-mārtaṇḍa-sambhūtam—born of Chhaya and Surya; namāmi—I bow; śanaiścaram—to Shani.
verses.translation: I bow to Shani, dark as sacred collyrium, son of Surya, elder brother of Yama, born of Chhaya and the solar lord.
verses.commentary: Shani is time, consequence, humility, and slow maturation. This verse is best used to cultivate patience, realism, service, and karmic honesty rather than fear-driven appeasement.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
अर्धकायं महावीर्यं चन्द्रादित्यविमर्दनम्।
सिंहिकागर्भसम्भूतं तं राहुं प्रणमाम्यहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
ardhakāyaṁ mahāvīryaṁ candrāditya vimardanam
siṁhikāgarbha sambhūtaṁ taṁ rāhuṁ praṇamāmyaham
verses.wordMeanings: ardha-kāyam—half-bodied; mahā-vīryam—of great force; candra-āditya-vimardanam—who disturbs sun and moon; siṁhikā-garbha-sambhūtam—born of Simhika; rāhum—to Rahu; praṇamāmi aham—I bow.
verses.translation: I bow to Rahu, half-bodied and immensely forceful, born of Simhika, whose eclipse power can obscure sun and moon.
verses.commentary: Rahu represents amplification, appetite, disruption, and shadow fascination. This verse can become a contemplative reminder to meet obsession with discernment and grounding.

verses.sanskritDevanagari:
पलाशपुष्पसङ्काशं तारकाग्रहमस्तकम्।
रौद्रं रौद्रात्मकं घोरं तं केतुं प्रणमाम्यहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
palāśapuṣpa saṅkāśaṁ tārakāgraha mastakam
raudraṁ raudrātmakaṁ ghoraṁ taṁ ketuṁ praṇamāmyaham
verses.wordMeanings: palāśa-puṣpa—palasha flower; saṅkāśam—shining like; tārakā-graha-mastakam—crowned among stars and grahas; raudram—fierce; raudrātmakam—of fierce nature; ghoram—intense; ketum—to Ketu; praṇamāmi aham—I bow.
verses.translation: I bow to Ketu, radiant like the palasha flower, intense and fierce in nature, subtle among the stellar and graha forces.
verses.commentary: Ketu symbolizes detachment, severance, inwardization, and moksha-oriented insight. In practice this verse supports simplification, introspection, and the willingness to release excess identity.
